26. In this event, we can refer to the case of Kani Chandra vs Nipendra Chandra, reported in 27 BLC (AD) 1 where the issue was the illegitimacy of a child, the plaintiff of a civil suit, wherein Kani Chandra Das being the son of Krishna Chandra and his wife Niroda Bala became plaintiff of the suit but the defendant claimed that Niroda left her house with one Kalu Sarder and Kani Chandra Das was not the son of Krishna Chandra Das rather he was an illegitimate son of Kalu Sarder having no entitlement to inherit the property left by Niroda. Though the case was civil in nature but the question was arisen regarding illegitimacy of the plaintiff, wherein it was held that an innocent child should not be victim of court's decision. The court has to consider diverse aspects including presumption under section 112 of the Evidence Act. In the case of Shyam Lal @ Kuldip vs Sanjeev Kumar and others, (2009) 12 SCC 454, it was observed that, 

 "Presumption cannot be displaced by mere balance of probabilities or any circumstances creating doubt. Even the evidence of adultery by wife which though amounts to very strong evidence, it, by itself, is quite sufficient to repel this presumption and will not justify finding of illegitimacy if husband has had access" 

 27. In the civilized society, if the parents who have access to each other, the question of legitimacy of child during continuance of the valid marriage, is undesirable to enquire into the paternity of child. Section 112 of the Evidence Act, is based on presumption of the public morality and public policy. It cannot be brushed aside straight way. Once the validity of marriages is proved, then there has been strong presumption about the legitimacy of children born out of that wedlock under section 112 of the Evidence Act. 

 30. Even though the Muhammadan Law has given importance on section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act which states that present Rule on the subject is to be found in the conclusive presumption raised in section 112 Indian Evidence Act. The Rule may be shortly states as follows: 

 (2) it is not proved that the claimant is the offspring of Zina [illicit intercourse] and (3) the circumstances are such that they do not rebut the presumption of paternity, an acknowledgement of paternity by the father is possible and effective.
